knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)

library(ggplot2)

# Model and source

```{r model-meta}
ui <- rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Ulaszek_2026_tafamidis_qsp"))
```

* Citation: `r ui$reference`
* Description: `r ui$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics18030367>
* Supplement (Lua model code, population-sampling R scripts, Simcyp
  simulation workbook): <https://www.mdpi.com/article/10.3390/pharmaceutics18030367/s1>

Ulaszek 2026 couples a Simcyp V23 whole-body PBPK model of tafamidis to a
six-ODE quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) model of tafamidis binding to
transthyretin (TTR) and of TTR turnover. The PBPK model is a forcing function:
its total plasma tafamidis concentration feeds the QSP model, with no feedback.
Only the QSP layer is packaged here. The PBPK layer relies on Simcyp database
physiology (organ volumes, blood flows, the ADAM absorption model) that the
paper does not publish, so it cannot be rebuilt from the published sources;
the total plasma concentration therefore enters as the time-varying covariate
`CP_TAFAMIDIS_UM`.

To drive the QSP model this article uses the paper's own PBPK output. The
supplementary simulation workbook contains the Simcyp plasma profile of each of
the 30 virtual subjects (sheet "Conc Profiles CSys(CPlasma)", in uM) for
80 mg tafamidis meglumine once daily. The first 21 days of those profiles,
resampled from the 0.254 h Simcyp grid to every fourth point (1.02 h), ship
with this article as `data/Ulaszek_2026_tafamidis_simcyp.csv`. Resampling
changes the steady-state unbound-to-total TTR ratio by less than 0.001
percentage points relative to the full-resolution profiles.

# Population

The QSP simulations use 30 virtual healthy men aged 30-40 years. Each subject
has a baseline TTR sampled from a normal distribution with the mean and SD that
Ingenbleek et al. report for this age and sex stratum (Section 2.4); the
baseline was split into a synthesis rate r and a degradation rate Tdeg
(baseline TTR = r / Tdeg) by an optimiser started from the Oppenheimer et al.
turnover estimates. Albumin is the Simcyp healthy-volunteer value for each
virtual subject (Table A2). The age range was chosen to match the only
multiple-dose tafamidis study (B3461056, 30 healthy men, Lockwood 2020) and the
radiolabelled TTR turnover studies. Women were not simulated.

The same information is available programmatically:

```{r population}
str(ui$population)
```

# Source trace

Every `ini()` value carries an in-file comment pointing to its source; this
table collects them.

| Equation / parameter | Value | Source location |
|---|---|---|
| `ksyn` (r) | 0.092565 uM/h (typical); per subject in the cohort table below | Supplementary R script `1_TTR sampling.R` (Oppenheimer average used as optimiser start); per-subject values: deposited Lua script `patient_synthesis_and_degradation_rates_table` |
| `kdeg` (Tdeg) | 0.015125 1/h (typical); per subject below | Section 2.4 (Oppenheimer 0.363 1/day); same R script and Lua table |
| `kdiss` | 0.0024 1/h | Table A2, 'Dissociation rate of unbound TTR' |
| `kreassoc` (paper `ka`) | 360,000 1/(uM^3 h) | Table A2, 'Association rate of unbound TTR' |
| `kdeg_monomer` (Mdeg) | 0.016 1/h | Table A2, 'Monomer degradation rate' |
| `kon1` | 16,200 1/(uM h) | Table A2 |
| `koff1` | 50.2 1/h (Nelson-based); 28.8 (Corazza) | Table A2 |
| `kon2` | 12,600 1/(uM h) | Table A2 |
| `koff2` | 2998.8 1/h (Nelson-based); 216 (Corazza) | Table A2 |
| `kon_alb` | 1000 1/(uM h) | Table A2 |
| `koff_alb` | 1800 1/h | Table A2 |
| `f_kdeg_bound` (s) | 0.735 | Deposited Lua script (`T_bound_deg = P[2]*0.735`); Section 2.3 Eq 4 and Table A2 give the approximation 0.75 |
| Albumin MW | 66,500 g/mol | Deposited Lua script (`getIndivHSA()/66500*1000000`) |
| Free tafamidis | `CP - (TTR1 + 2 TTR2 + Alb1)` | Eq 11 |
| Single-bound complex | ODE | Eq 5 |
| Double-bound complex | ODE | Eq 6 |
| Free TTR tetramer | ODE | Eq 7 |
| TTR monomer | ODE | Eq 8 |
| Tafamidis-albumin complex | ODE | Eq 9 |
| Free albumin | ODE | Eq 10 |
| Initial free TTR | `ksyn / kdeg` (r / Tdeg) | Eq 2; Lua `odeInitStep` |
| Initial monomer | `(kdiss / ka * r / Tdeg)^(1/4)` | Eq A1; Lua `odeInitStep` |

# Virtual cohort

The per-subject synthesis and degradation rates are copied from the deposited
Simcyp Lua script; the albumin values are the "Individual albumin
concentration" column of the workbook's "PD Individual Parameters" sheet (uM),
converted to g/L with the 66,500 g/mol molecular weight that the script uses.

The Discussion's "low-TTR patient (3.85 uM)" and "high-TTR patient (7.51 uM)"
are subjects 2 and 21:

```{r low-high}
low_id <- cohort$id[which.min(abs(cohort$ttr0 - 3.85))]
high_id <- cohort$id[which.min(abs(cohort$ttr0 - 7.51))]
stopifnot(low_id == 2, high_id == 21)
```

# Tafamidis driver profiles

```{r driver}
driver_wide <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "Ulaszek_2026_tafamidis_simcyp.csv"))
driver <- driver_wide |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "id", names_prefix = "id", values_to = "CP_TAFAMIDIS_UM") |>
  mutate(id = as.integer(id)) |>
  arrange(id, time)

mw_tafamidis <- 308.12 # g/mol, free acid (Table A1)
```

## PKNCA check of the driver against Table 2

The profiles are the paper's own PBPK output, so their NCA should match the
PBPK predictions the paper tabulates. Table 2 reports the predicted day-7
values of study B3461056 (80 mg once daily) and the single-dose values of study
B3461054 (fasted). The workbook doses at the Simcyp grid points nearest each
24 h multiple; the nominal 24 h dosing times are used here.

```{r driver-nca}
dose_df <- tibble(
  id = rep(1:30, each = 21),
  time = rep(24 * (0:20), times = 30),
  amt = 48.8, # mg tafamidis per 80 mg tafamidis meglumine (Section 2.3)
  treatment = "80 mg QD"
)

conc_df <- driver |>
  transmute(id, time, conc = CP_TAFAMIDIS_UM * mw_tafamidis, treatment = "80 mg QD")

conc_obj <- PKNCAconc(conc_df, conc ~ time | treatment + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
intervals <- data.frame(
  start = c(0, 144),
  end = c(24, 168),
  cmax = TRUE,
  tmax = TRUE,
  aucint.last = c(FALSE, TRUE)
)
nca_res <- pk.nca(PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))

simulated_nca <- as.data.frame(nca_res) |>
  mutate(treatment = ifelse(start == 0, "Single dose (day 1)", "Day 7")) |>
  select(treatment, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  # The interval AUC (144-168 h, interpolated to the bounds) is reported
  # under the auclast label that ncaComparisonTable() knows.
  mutate(PPTESTCD = ifelse(PPTESTCD == "aucint.last", "auclast", PPTESTCD))

published <- tibble::tribble(
  ~treatment, ~cmax, ~tmax, ~auclast,
  # Table 2, B3461056 day 7, PREDICTED medians: AUC144-168h 179,721 ng*h/mL,
  # Cmax 9085 ng/mL, Tmax 1.90 h
  "Day 7", 9085, 1.90, 179721,
  # Table 2, B3461054 single dose fasted, PREDICTED: Cmax geometric mean
  # 3586 ng/mL, Tmax median 2.26 h
  "Single dose (day 1)", 3586, 2.26, NA
)

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = simulated_nca,
  reference = published,
  by = "treatment",
  units = c(cmax = "ng/mL", tmax = "h", auclast = "ng*h/mL"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(
  cmp,
  caption = paste(
    "Driver NCA (median of the 30 workbook profiles) against the PBPK",
    "predictions of Ulaszek 2026 Table 2. AUClast is the day-7 AUC over",
    "144-168 h."
  )
)
```

```{r driver-nca-check}
day7 <- as.data.frame(nca_res) |> filter(start == 144)
med7 <- tapply(day7$PPORRES, day7$PPTESTCD, median)
# The driver is a single 30-subject Simcyp trial while Table 2 summarises the
# paper's own predicted cohort; the exposure scale must agree closely.
stopifnot(
  abs(med7[["aucint.last"]] / 179721 - 1) < 0.10,
  abs(med7[["cmax"]] / 9085 - 1) < 0.10
)
```

Cmax and AUC agree within 4%. The day-7 Tmax is the one starred row: the
shipped profiles are on a 1.02 h grid and the workbook doses at 143.99 h rather
than at the nominal 144 h, so a Tmax difference of about 0.4 h is within the
grid's resolution rather than a difference in exposure.

# Simulation: 80 mg tafamidis meglumine once daily

```{r solve-80}
ev <- driver |>
  left_join(select(cohort, id, ALB), by = "id")
per_subject <- select(cohort, ksyn, kdeg)

solve_qsp <- function(model, events, params) {
  rxode2::rxSolve(
    model,
    events = events,
    params = params,
    covsInterpolation = "linear",
    atol = 1e-10,
    rtol = 1e-8,
    maxsteps = 1e6,
    returnType = "data.frame"
  )
}

sim80 <- solve_qsp(ui, ev, per_subject)
```

## Replicate Figure 3

```{r fig3, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
state_labels <- c(
  complex_ttr1 = "Single tafamidis-TTR complex",
  complex_ttr2 = "Double tafamidis-TTR complex",
  ttr_free = "Free TTR",
  ttr_monomer = "TTR monomer",
  complex_albumin = "Tafamidis-albumin complex",
  ttr_bound = "Bound TTR",
  ttr_total = "Total TTR"
)
sim80 |>
  select(id, time, all_of(names(state_labels))) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(id, time), names_to = "state") |>
  group_by(time, state) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(state = factor(state_labels[state], levels = state_labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, value, colour = state)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Time (h)",
    y = "Mean concentration (uM)",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Replicates the first 21 days of Figure 3 of Ulaszek 2026 (Nelson-based binding constants)."
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))
```

## Identity check against the deposited simulation

The workbook's "PD Custom ODE" sheet holds the Simcyp solution of the same
equations for the same 30 subjects. Both solves share the driver profile and
every parameter, so the population means must agree to within integrator and
resampling error. The reference values are the workbook's population means at
five times on the shipped grid.

```{r identity}
workbook_means <- tibble::tribble(
  ~time, ~complex_ttr1, ~complex_ttr2, ~ttr_free, ~ttr_monomer, ~complex_albumin, ~albumin,
  2.0352, 4.41014, 0.322302, 0.845401, 0.00766591, 6.55205, 674.383,
  24.4224, 4.69780, 0.353242, 0.897627, 0.00840514, 6.70954, 674.225,
  168.9216, 5.50736, 1.301401, 0.318329, 0.00634387, 20.76375, 660.171,
  336.8256, 5.68405, 1.336763, 0.331020, 0.00640140, 20.71367, 660.221,
  503.7120, 5.94709, 0.864625, 0.570647, 0.00677440, 13.01677, 667.918
)

states <- setdiff(names(workbook_means), "time")
model_means <- sim80 |>
  filter(round(time, 4) %in% round(workbook_means$time, 4)) |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(states), mean), .groups = "drop")

identity <- workbook_means |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "state", values_to = "workbook") |>
  left_join(
    pivot_longer(model_means, -time, names_to = "state", values_to = "model"),
    by = c("time", "state")
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (model / workbook - 1))

identity |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(`max abs % diff` = max(abs(pct_diff))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Model vs workbook population means over the five check times.")

stopifnot(
  nrow(identity) == 30,
  all(abs(identity$pct_diff[identity$state != "ttr_monomer"]) < 1)
)
```

The five drug-bound, TTR and albumin states agree to well under 1%. The
monomer does not: the workbook monomer is 10-14% below this solve whenever drug
is present, and it settles at 0.0127 uM rather than the 0.0143 uM that the
printed monomer equation (Eq 8) gives at baseline, even after the drug washes
out. The baseline monomer here equals Eq A1 exactly:

```{r monomer-baseline}
base <- sim80 |> filter(time == 0)
eq_a1 <- with(cohort, (0.0024 / 360000 * ksyn / kdeg)^(1 / 4))
stopifnot(max(abs(base$ttr_monomer / eq_a1 - 1)) < 1e-8)
```

The deposited equations reproduce every other workbook state, so the monomer
offset is a property of the Simcyp solve of that one state. The monomer
carries well under 1% of total TTR, so the offset does not move any other
state.

## The 33% rise in total TTR

The paper calibrates the bound-complex clearance so that total TTR rises by
about 33% at steady state (Section 2.3). The text derives the scaling factor
analytically as 1/1.33, about 0.75, which assumes that all TTR is drug-bound and
that monomer loss is negligible. The deposited script uses 0.735. Under the full
model, with 5% of TTR still unbound and a monomer drain, 0.735 gives the 33%
rise and 0.75 falls short:

```{r ttr-rise}
rise <- function(sim) {
  sim |>
    filter(time == 0 | round(time, 4) == 503.712) |>
    group_by(time) |>
    summarise(ttr_total = mean(ttr_total), .groups = "drop") |>
    with(ttr_total[2] / ttr_total[1] - 1)
}
ui_075 <- ui |> rxode2::ini(f_kdeg_bound = 0.75)
rise_0735 <- rise(sim80)
rise_075 <- rise(solve_qsp(ui_075, ev, per_subject))

tibble(
  `Scaling factor s` = c("0.735", "0.75"),
  `Rise in mean total TTR, day 21 (%)` = 100 * c(rise_0735, rise_075)
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)

# Workbook: mean total TTR rises from 5.542 uM to 7.382 uM by day 21
# (+33.2%), the same value as on day 91.
stopifnot(
  abs(100 * rise_0735 - 33.2) < 0.5,
  rise_075 < rise_0735 - 0.01
)
```

## Albumin mass balance

Albumin has no synthesis or loss in the model, so free albumin plus the
tafamidis-albumin complex must stay at each subject's input albumin.

```{r albumin-balance}
alb_check <- sim80 |>
  left_join(select(cohort, id, alb_um), by = "id") |>
  mutate(rel = (albumin + complex_albumin) / alb_um - 1)
# Rounding of the cohort albumin to two decimals is the only difference.
stopifnot(max(abs(alb_check$rel)) < 1e-5)
```

# Corazza-based binding constants (Figure A2)

The paper runs the model with a second set of binding constants taken
directly from Corazza 2019 (`koff1` 28.8 and `koff2` 216 1/h). Tighter binding
shifts tafamidis from the single-bound into the double-bound complex.

```{r figA2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
ui_corazza <- ui |> rxode2::ini(koff1 = 28.8, koff2 = 216)
sim80_cor <- solve_qsp(ui_corazza, ev, per_subject)

bind_rows(
  Nelson = sim80,
  Corazza = sim80_cor,
  .id = "set"
) |>
  select(set, id, time, complex_ttr1, complex_ttr2, ttr_free) |>
  pivot_longer(c(complex_ttr1, complex_ttr2, ttr_free), names_to = "state") |>
  group_by(set, time, state) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(state = state_labels[state]) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, value, colour = state)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~set) +
  labs(
    x = "Time (h)",
    y = "Mean concentration (uM)",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Replicates Figure A2 (Corazza) against Figure 3 (Nelson) of Ulaszek 2026."
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ss_bound <- function(sim) {
  sim |>
    filter(time >= 480) |>
    summarise(across(c(complex_ttr1, complex_ttr2), mean))
}
stopifnot(
  ss_bound(sim80_cor)$complex_ttr2 > ss_bound(sim80)$complex_ttr2,
  ss_bound(sim80_cor)$complex_ttr1 < ss_bound(sim80)$complex_ttr1
)
```

# Dose sensitivity (Figure 4)

Figure 4 plots the steady-state unbound-to-total TTR ratio for 20, 40, 60, 80
and 160 mg tafamidis meglumine once daily: the population mean (with SD) and
the low-TTR and high-TTR subjects. The workbook holds only the 80 mg profiles,
so the other doses are approximated by scaling them with dose, which assumes
linear tafamidis pharmacokinetics over this range. The ratio is averaged over
the last dosing interval (day 21).

```{r fig4-solve}
doses <- c(20, 40, 60, 80, 160)

ratio_by_dose <- function(model) {
  bind_rows(lapply(doses, function(d) {
    ev_d <- mutate(ev, CP_TAFAMIDIS_UM = CP_TAFAMIDIS_UM * d / 80)
    solve_qsp(model, ev_d, per_subject) |>
      filter(time >= 480) |>
      group_by(id) |>
      summarise(ratio = 100 * mean(ttr_unbound_ratio), .groups = "drop") |>
      mutate(dose = d)
  }))
}
fig4 <- bind_rows(
  Nelson = ratio_by_dose(ui),
  Corazza = ratio_by_dose(ui_corazza),
  .id = "set"
)

fig4_summary <- fig4 |>
  group_by(set, dose) |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(ratio),
    sd = sd(ratio),
    low = ratio[id == low_id],
    high = ratio[id == high_id],
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

The published values come from the Discussion where it states them
(population mean 4.59% at 60 mg and 2.19% at 80 mg; low-TTR subject 2.55% at
60 mg; high-TTR subject 3.86% at 80 mg) and were otherwise digitised by the
maintainers from Figure 4 (bar tops measured on the published image; the
digitised bars reproduce the four Discussion values to within 0.2 percentage
points).

```{r fig4-compare}
paper_fig4 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~dose, ~mean, ~low, ~high,
  20, 32.7, 24.9, 45.4,
  40, 11.4, 6.83, 19.5,
  60, 4.59, 2.55, 8.17,
  80, 2.19, 1.10, 3.86
)

fig4_cmp <- fig4_summary |>
  select(set, dose, mean, low, high) |>
  pivot_longer(c(mean, low, high), names_to = "group", values_to = "model") |>
  inner_join(
    pivot_longer(paper_fig4, -dose, names_to = "group", values_to = "paper"),
    by = c("dose", "group")
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (model / paper - 1))

fig4_cmp |>
  select(set, dose, group, paper, model, pct_diff) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = set, values_from = c(model, pct_diff)) |>
  arrange(group, dose) |>
  rename(
    `Dose (mg)` = dose,
    Group = group,
    `Paper (%)` = paper,
    `Nelson set (%)` = model_Nelson,
    `Corazza set (%)` = model_Corazza,
    `Nelson % diff` = pct_diff_Nelson,
    `Corazza % diff` = pct_diff_Corazza
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Unbound-to-total TTR ratio at steady state against Figure 4 of Ulaszek 2026.")
```

```{r fig4-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
fig4_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(dose), mean, fill = set)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd),
    position = position_dodge(0.8),
    width = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = paper_fig4,
    aes(factor(dose), mean),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 4,
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Tafamidis meglumine dose (mg once daily)",
    y = "Unbound / total TTR ratio (%)",
    fill = "Binding constants",
    caption = "Replicates the population-mean bars of Figure 4 of Ulaszek 2026 (crosses: published values)."
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The Corazza-based constants reproduce Figure 4 to within 15% for every bar
(within 1% for the 20 mg mean), with the largest shortfalls at 60-80 mg where
the published ratios are smallest and most sensitive to the dose-scaled
drivers; the Nelson-based constants,
which the deposited script and Figure 3 use, give unbound fractions 1.8 to
3.9 times the published values at 60-80 mg. Figure 4 was therefore evidently generated with
the Corazza set, although the paper does not say so.

```{r fig4-check}
cor_rows <- filter(fig4_cmp, set == "Corazza")
nel_80 <- filter(fig4_cmp, set == "Nelson", dose == 80, group == "mean")
stopifnot(
  # Structural: the Corazza set lands on the published bars.
  abs(median(cor_rows$pct_diff)) < 10,
  max(abs(cor_rows$pct_diff)) < 25,
  # The Nelson set does not (5.5% against 2.19% at 80 mg).
  nel_80$pct_diff > 100
)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **PBPK layer not extracted.** The Simcyp V23 whole-body PBPK model of
  tafamidis is not reproducible from the published sources: organ volumes,
  blood flows and the ADAM absorption rate are Simcyp database outputs, and
  Table A1 prints only the compound inputs (physicochemical properties,
  fu 0.008, B:P 0.55, tissue Kp values, Peff, total clearance 0.262 L/h,
  Vss 0.169 L/kg). Total plasma tafamidis is a covariate instead.
* **Driver profiles from the supplement.** The article drives the model with
  the paper's own Simcyp plasma profiles (30 subjects, first 21 days of
  80 mg once daily) rather than with an independent PK model; the PKNCA check
  above confirms they match the PBPK predictions of Table 2.
* **Scaling factor 0.735, not 0.75.** Section 2.3 and Table A2 give the
  bound-complex clearance factor as 1/1.33, about 0.75, an analytic
  approximation. The deposited Simcyp script uses 0.735, and that value
  reproduces the 33% rise in the full model and the workbook outputs, so the
  model carries 0.735.
* **Typical `ksyn` and `kdeg`.** The model's default synthesis and degradation
  rates are the Oppenheimer averages that seeded the per-subject split
  (baseline TTR 6.12 uM). The paper never simulates a "typical" subject; its
  results always use the 30 per-subject pairs, which this article supplies
  through `params`.
* **Binding constants.** The model defaults to the Nelson-based set, which the
  deposited script and Figure 3 use. Figure 4 matches the Corazza-based set
  instead (see above); switch with
  `ini(koff1 = 28.8, koff2 = 216)`.
* **Monomer.** The workbook's monomer trajectory is 10-14% below the solution
  of the printed Eq 8; every other state matches. The model follows the
  printed equation.
* **Dose scaling for Figure 4.** The non-80 mg drivers are the 80 mg profiles
  scaled by dose, assuming linear pharmacokinetics; Figure 4 used separate
  Simcyp runs at each dose.
* **Monomer degradation rate.** Table A2 states that no data exist for
  `kdeg_monomer`; the paper assumes it equals the average TTR degradation rate.
* **No variability model.** The paper fits no IIV or residual error; the
  between-subject spread comes only from the per-subject turnover rates,
  albumin and drug exposure.
